core: Working definition of compound growth: growth earned on both the original amount and previously earned growth (attributed to Investor.gov and CFPB)
The compounding engine: each period's growth joins the base for the next period, with the original $1,000 at 7% for 10 years worked example
The rule of 72: years to double approximately 72 divided by the annual rate, stated as an approximation
Starting early: small regular amounts grow large because time compounds them; original early-vs-late comparison
Compound growth and debt: the same engine grows unpaid balances (flip side); debt-management referenced as sibling topic only
Honest framing: compound growth rewards time and punishes delay; no guarantee of gains

Compounding frequency concept (yearly, monthly, quarterly) as one of the components

claims.claim: Compound growth is growth earned on both the original amount and previously earned growth; Investor.gov defines compound interest as interest paid on principal and on accumulated interest.
Interest is calculated on the principal plus previously accumulated interest, so a balance grows on its own (CFPB mechanics of interest-on-interest).

The four components of compounding are principal, interest rate, compounding frequency, and time horizon; the longer the time horizon, the more interest payments can be made and the larger the ending value.

The rule of 72 estimates the time it takes money to double by dividing 72 by the annual rate; it is a shortcut or back-of-the-envelope approximation, most accurate at lower/moderate rates, and applies to compound-interest situations rather than simple interest.
Because each period's growth joins the base, earlier contributions compound for more periods; at a fixed rate, starting earlier can outgrow contributing more later.
Compound growth applies to debt as well as savings: an unpaid balance grows on its own because growth is calculated on the amount owed plus accumulated growth.

The mechanism of compounding is arithmetic: it requires a positive rate to grow, and does not guarantee gains; CFI's characterization of compound interest as 'essentially a risk-free way to generate gains' was not adopted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: CFI describes compound interest as 'essentially a risk-free way to generate gains'.
positions: CFI: compounding mechanism is relatively riskless compared with other investments
Honest framing: compounding is arithmetic that amplifies whatever rate applies; it does not guarantee gains, and unpaid debt compounds against the borrower
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson adopts the honest framing and does not repeat CFI's risk-free claim; the lesson states that a zero or negative rate changes the outcome and that the mechanism promises nothing.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Precision of the rule of 72 at different rates.
positions: Some sources present the rule as a quick estimate
CFI notes it is more accurate at lower rates
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the rule explicitly as an approximation and notes it is most accurate at moderate rates, so no false precision is implied.

positions: The personal-finance curriculum names the concept 'compound growth' because it applies to savings and debt alike
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the curriculum name 'compound growth', attributes the underlying definition to Investor.gov and CFPB, and notes the interest topic owns interest mechanics.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate (e.g., compound growth as 'a label on a toolbox drawer', 'students use concepts to organize information') contained no verifiable factual claims and was discarded as editorial intent only.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate draft with source-verified content.
Original worked example ($1,000 at 7% for 10 years) arithmetic verified by computation: final balance $1,967.15.
Original early-vs-late example (Priya vs Dana at 7%) arithmetic verified by computation: $80,237 vs $67,676 at age 60.
Original rule-of-72 applications verified: 72/7 about 10.3 years; 72/6 = 12 years; 72/24 = 3 years.
